A bound volume with pages that still turn. The cover is gone or the title is no longer legible. It does not matter what it was about. It matters that someone carried it this far and did not burn it for warmth. The words inside are someone else's thoughts, preserved by accident. That is enough.

A tube of drafting paper, the kind an engineer carried before the exchange. The blueprint inside is faded but legible — floor plans, elevation marks, a structure that may or may not still stand. The person who carried this believed the drawing was worth more than food. They may have been right.

A padded headset with a wired microphone on a flexible boom. The ear cups are cracked leather over foam that has gone to dust. The cable ends in a connector that fits the bunker's intercom panel. It still transmits. The person who wore this one heard orders and gave them back. The orders no longer matter. The headset still works.

A nine-millimetre sidearm in a worn holster. The bluing is gone from the slide and the grip tape is peeling. Seven rounds in the magazine. The safety still clicks. The person who carried this one kept it oiled, kept it loaded, kept it pointed at the ground until the ground asked for something else. The pistol does not know what it is for anymore.

A folded surgical mask in a torn paper wrapper. The elastic ear loops are still intact. It will not stop radiation. It will stop the things that come out of a patient's lungs when the lungs are still working. The person who wore this one put it on before every procedure. The procedure is what the mask is for.

A surgical scalpel in a sealed blister pack, the blade still bright under the foil. Number ten blade, the kind used for initial incisions. The handle is lightweight alloy, the kind that does not corrode. Someone sterilized this before packing it. Someone believed it would be needed again.

A pair of surgical forceps, stainless steel, the serrated tips still aligned. The hinge moves without grit. They are the kind used to clamp and to hold, to pull what should not remain inside a body. They have been cleaned and wrapped in gauze. The gauze is yellowed but dry.

A sealed packet of absorbable suture material, the kind that dissolves in tissue over three weeks. The needle is swaged, the thread still coated. Five packets to a pack. The expiry date is illegible but the seal has not been breached. The suture will hold a wound closed long enough for the body to do the rest.

Two aluminium tags on a beaded chain, the stamped letters still legible. A name, a number, a blood type, a faith that is no longer practised. The chain was cut, not broken. Someone removed these from the person they belonged to. Someone carried them out. The tags are light. What they weigh is not the aluminium.

A sack of broken concrete, the rebar stubs bent and rusted at the edges. Pulled from a collapsed wall or a shattered overpass, it is the kind of material that was a building yesterday and is fill today. Heavy. Abrasive. The bunker uses it for ballast, for mortar aggregate, for the things that need weight and do not need to be pretty.

A sealed glass bottle of industrial solvent, the label long gone but the contents still sharp enough to sting the eyes through the cap. Pulled from a laboratory shelf or a cleaning supply cabinet that someone forgot to loot. It dissolves grease, thins paint, and marks paper with a line that does not fade. Three tenths of a kilo, worth five. The bunker uses it when ordinary water is not enough.

A plastic toner cartridge from a laser printer that no longer works, the drum scratched and the powder compartment empty. It is light, the size of a shoe, and it still smells faintly of carbon. The residual toner dust inside can be suspended in water and used as ink — a dark, even line that holds on paper longer than most things written after the exchange. Worth three. Office salvage.

A fist-sized piece of mineral broken from a exposed stratum or a collapsed mine shaft. The colour runs from rust-red to chalk-white depending on what it is. Heavy for its size, it can be ground into a coarse pigment or dissolved for chemical use. The archive values it for ink. The forge values it for flux. Half a kilo, worth two.

A sealed glass vial of blood, the type written on a strip of tape that is starting to peel. Taken from a medical supply cabinet or a field kit that someone left behind. It is not useful as medicine in this form. It is useful as a record — proof of who was here, what they carried in their veins, and whether the water they drank was clean. A quarter kilo, worth four to the right buyer.

A jar of dark organic residue scraped from a compost heap, a drainage channel, or the inside of a water filter that has been running too long. It smells like earth and something older. The archive boils it down for a sepia-toned ink that fades slowly and reads well in low light. The greenhouse spreads it on soil that has given up. Three tenths of a kilo, worth two.
A simple gold band, scratched by years of manual labor. It has no gem, just a faint inscription inside worn down by friction against skin: 'Always, M.'
A color print from before the war, corners softened by grease and handling. A family sits together on a porch in summer sunlight that feels impossible now.
A black-and-white portrait creased down the middle. One figure has been touched so many times that the emulsion has worn away to white paper.
A velvet-covered album with half its pages torn out. The remaining prints show birthday parties, snowy streets, and houses with unboarded windows.
A piece of heavy construction paper showing a yellow sun, a blue house with curly smoke, and three smiling stick figures holding hands.
A stuffed bear with one button eye and a patched ear. The fur smells of attic dust and old laundry detergent.
An index card stained with butter and vanilla, bearing handwritten notes for rye bread. In the margin, in shaky pencil: 'When flour is short, add boiled potato.'
A tin box with painted blue cornflowers, packed with handwritten cards spanning forty years of meals, family birthdays, and wartime ration substitutions.
A single red wool mitten with a safety pin still attached to the cuff where it used to clip to a coat sleeve. The wool is coarse but hand-knit.
A long red scarf knitted with uneven stitches, frayed at the tassels. Bright enough to spot across a crowded pre-war train platform.
A heavy petrol lighter with an etched regimental crest on the lid. The flint still sparks and the wick is charred black from lighting wood stoves.
A bronze military medal in a satin-lined presentation box. The ribbon is faded olive drab, and the clasp has never been pinned to a dress uniform.
A black oilcloth notebook filled with pencil entries: grocery tallies, tire pressure notes, and promises to call relatives that abruptly end on Day Zero.
A brass mortise key stamped '4B' on a worn leather fob. The apartment building it opened collapsed into rubble decades ago, but the key remains polished.
A heavy brass whistle with a dried pea inside that still rattles. Used to signal shift changes and blast evacuations across the municipal foundry floor.
An upside-down pinned watch with a red seconds hand for taking pulse readings. The crystal is cracked, but the spring mechanism still ticks cleanly.
A silver pocket watch that stopped at four minutes past eight. The back cover is engraved with initials and an anniversary date from before the Exchange.
A stainless steel vernier caliper in a wooden case. The thumb roller moves smoothly, measuring thousandths of an inch with uncompromising pre-war precision.
A bamboo and celluloid calculating rule in a leather sheath. Used to calculate structural loads, radiation half-lives, and generator outputs without power.
A numbered brass token stamped 'Shift 3 / #142'. Miners hung them on the lamp-house board on their way underground so the surface knew who was below.
A cloth-bound ledger tracking bushels of winter wheat, rainfall averages, and livestock weights across twenty seasons of peacetime soil.
A nickel-plated ticket punch that cuts a distinctive star-shaped hole. The lever still snaps with crisp, practiced rhythm.
Heavy split-cowhide gloves stained black with motor oil and diesel. The right index finger has been mended three times with copper wire.
A rubber-faced wooden stamp reading 'EXCELLENT WORK' in block capitals, with dried red ink encrusted in the grain of the handle.
A thin slip of printed paper for the 7:15 AM crosstown route, punched twice and folded into a tiny square. The date is forty-eight hours before Day Zero.
The back of a gas receipt listing: 'Milk, oats, 1/2 lb butter, coffee, birthday candles.' Four of the five items are crossed off with firm pencil strokes.
A speckled blue enamel tin mug, chipped down to black iron along the rim where someone's teeth rested while drinking tea in the morning.
A brown pocket comb with three missing teeth. Pulled from a bathroom medicine cabinet that survived the blast wave intact.
A cardboard matchbook advertising 'Silver Star Diner — Open 24 Hours'. Twelve cardboard matches remain, unspent.
A purple-ink grocery receipt for three cans of peaches and a loaf of bread, dated an ordinary Tuesday afternoon before the sirens.
A small cast-brass clover souvenir charm attached to a split ring. Smooth to the touch from years in a jacket pocket.
A stiff leather doctor's satchel containing clean clamps, swaddling cloths, and an umbilical scissor oiled and wrapped in linen.
A heavy canvas-bound ledger recording coastal weather, tides, and the final entries tracking navigational lights going dark one by one across the gulf.
A pad of numbered emergency transit coupons marked 'Sector Priority Evacuation'. Most were never torn from the stub.
A transistor radio encased in bright yellow impact plastic, tuned to the emergency broadcast frequency that fell silent thirty years ago.
A pair of notched stainless steel tags on a beaded chain, stamped with an army serial number and blood type.
A set of military tags with a small gold religious medal taped securely to the back of the primary tag.
A bundle of postmarked letters tied with hemp twine, never sorted into mailboxes on the morning the missiles launched.
A solid steel surgical scalpel with a balanced handle and interchangeable blade slot, sterilized and preserved in oiled chamois.
A medical stethoscope with flexible rubber tubing and a cold chrome chestpiece that has listened to hundreds of human chests.
A clinical acoustic stethoscope in good working condition, essential for triage and pulse diagnostics in the infirmary.
A wax-sealed paper packet containing twenty-five unhybridized tomato seeds kept dry and shielded from fallout radiation.
A sealed military trauma pouch with sterile pressure bandages, tourniquet, and antiseptic wipes packed for combat triage.
Thickened sky-layer armor plate designed to withstand falling structural debris and acid rain fallout.

A heavy cast iron collar machined to brace tunnel sections and shaft walls against ground pressure. The shoulders are drilled for anchor bolts and the surface is rough from the sand mold. The Silent Foundry delivers these in batches of six and does not ask what they are shoring up. The Sump Dredgers and the salt chamber workers both use them. Underground, a bracket is the difference between a collapse and a shift change.

A precision-cast alloy bushing and hinge bracket for pressure-rated doors and airlock bulkheads. The tolerances are tight enough that the threads are smooth to the touch. The Foundry makes these to specification from a technical drawing that has been copied so many times the numerals are barely legible. They work. The blast door in the Garrison command post still seats clean after forty years because the fitting was made right.

An anchor shoe cast to stabilize subsiding foundation columns in lower shelter blocks. The base plate is wide and the collar angle is adjustable with a set screw. The Foundry engraves a lot number into every one so the structural records can trace which shoe is under which column. In a shelter that cannot be abandoned, a failing column is not an engineering problem. It is a counting problem.

A cast iron sleeve coupling for joining heavy power conduits and steam lines between bunker sectors. The flanges are drilled for six bolts and the bore is machined to accept the standard conduit diameter used in pre-war civil construction. The coupling does not care whether it is carrying electricity or steam. The thing on either side of it does.

A set of high-carbon alloy stamping dies for reshaping and reworking workshop metal stock. The die faces are hardened and ground to mirror finish. When a press or a forming machine loses its die to a broken edge, the machine is worthless until a replacement arrives. The Foundry makes these one set at a time. They are worth what the workshop that needs them is worth.

Hexagonal tool-steel rods for regrinding rock drills and salt-mine augers. The blanks arrive in the Foundry's wrapped paper and the steel is hard enough to scratch a thumbnail. A blunt drill in a salt mine or a borehole costs a shift. A set of blanks costs a negotiation with the Foundry. The Sump Dredgers have standing credit for blanks because the Foundry needs their heavy lead for the casting pots.

A refractory-lined shell for replacing worn cupola and smelter crucibles. The lining is compressed and fired ceramic that can tolerate the Foundry's maximum pour temperature for sixty heats before it needs replacing. A cracked crucible mid-pour is the Foundry's worst accident scenario. The spare sits in the stock rack behind the tuyeres, never touched, always checked.

A precision hydraulic collar for pharmaceutical compactors and workshop hydraulic presses. The bore is lapped to a fine finish and the seal groove is cut for an O-ring that must be replaced each time the collar is disassembled. The Foundry makes one tolerance class finer than strictly necessary because the person who specified these once watched a poorly-fitted collar blow a press ram through a wall.

A split cast-iron bearing housing for heavy machine tool spindles and conveyor shafting. The bore is bored and line-reamed to accept a standard roller bearing race. The halves are matched, drilled, and pinned so they cannot be swapped or reversed. Each housing is stamped with the machine it was sized for. Swapping housings from different machines is how bearings fail in the middle of a production run.

A sectional cast iron grate for solid-fuel furnaces and boiler fireboxes. The bar spacing is set to let ash fall through without dropping unburned fuel. The Foundry replaces grates on a burn-through schedule: one bad section and the fire goes uneven; two bad sections and the combustion chamber develops a hot spot that warps the firebox shell. The grate is the cheapest part of a furnace. A warped firebox is not.

A sealed cast cylinder for outdoor instrument housings — barometers, anemometers, and recording thermometers. The Foundry makes these for the weather stations that survived the Exchange, most of which are still transmitting to nobody. The canister is waterproof and radiation-resistant. The instrument inside it may or may not be. The Foundry is responsible for the housing. The instrument is somebody else's problem.
Chilled lead-iron defensive shot canister used in automated bunker deadfall traps and perimeter barriers.

Rough-cast cylindrical billets for machining into custom housing shells and protective casings. The castings come out of the sand mold slightly oversized on all surfaces, waiting for the lathe. The Electrician uses them to make junction boxes that are not supposed to be junction boxes. The Mechanic uses them for things that are not supposed to be anything at all. That is what blanks are for.
Black rutabaga root cuttings with deep dormant eyes. Survives frost and damp soil that would rot ordinary roots.

A knobbled, ash-grey tuber the size of a fist, dense with starch and slightly bitter when eaten raw. Cooked, it softens to a mealy texture that fills the stomach in a way that flour cannot. The Botanist selected this strain for cold tolerance and short growing cycle. It does not need much light and it does not need much warmth. It needs patience. The patience of a person who cannot afford to lose a crop.

A small cloth packet of ash-grain seed, labeled in the Botanist's handwriting with a lot number and germination date. The seed is a winter-adapted cereal bred from several ancestors and selected over four generations of post-Exchange growing for tolerance to low light and contaminated soil. It does not produce much. It produces reliably. In the greenhouse, reliable is everything.

A sheaf of coarse-stalked grain with small dense heads, the hull still on. The grain is bitter and needs double boiling to leach out the tannins before it can be eaten comfortably. Made into flour it bakes into a dense, dark bread that lasts four days before going stale. The Botanist calls it food. The steward calls it sufficient. The children call it the bread that is not Tuesday bread, which is not an improvement.

A glass vial of mycelium culture rather than true seed — the Botanist calls it a seed because the concept is easier to communicate. The culture produces the glowing bracket mushroom that grows in the tunnel sections, providing navigational light and protein paste for the infirmary. Handle the vial at room temperature and do not shake it. The mycelium does not forgive rough treatment.
Luminescent fungal caps with a mild sedative effect. Harvested for calm-inducing teas and pharma extraction.

A sealed ampoule of algae starter culture in nutrient solution. The Botanist grows it in the UV-lit tank behind the pump room in thin green sheets that can be dried, ground, and added to grain flour to increase the protein yield by thirty percent. It smells of cold water and something else that nobody has been able to name. The smell goes away when it is dried. Mostly.
Thick protein-rich green paste skimmed from greenhouse cultivation basins. Bitter but life-sustaining.
Rooted herbal cuttings wrapped in damp sphagnum moss. Supplies the shelter dispensary with natural antipyretics.
Aromatic bundle of harvested fever-bark and dried yarrow leaves. Brewed to reduce fever and cleanse wounds.

A small paper envelope of mixed leafy vegetable seeds — varieties selected for dense nutrition per square centimeter and fast harvest cycle. The Botanist grows these in the shallowest greenhouse beds and harvests them continuously, a few leaves at a time, rather than pulling the whole plant. Fresh greens are rare enough that their distribution is tracked on the same board as the medical supplies.
Crisp, peppery green leaves packed with essential vitamin C. The primary shelter defense against scurvy.

A packet of cold-adapted oilseed, selected for high oil content per gram of seed. The Botanist presses the harvest in a small screw press the mechanic built from salvaged parts. The oil is pale green and slightly bitter and is used in cooking, as lamp fuel, and as a mechanical lubricant when nothing better is available. One crop cycle from these seeds produces enough oil to matter.

A handful of small oily seeds, green-grey and dense. The press yields about thirty percent by weight as oil. What is left after pressing is a high-protein cake that the Botanist mixes into the grain bread to increase its caloric density. The children do not like it. They eat it anyway. The steward makes sure of that.

A paper envelope of legume seeds bred for nitrogen fixation in contaminated soil and for production in low-light conditions. The Botanist uses them as a cover crop between grain cycles to restore the greenhouse beds without chemical fertilizer. They also produce a small yield of edible pods. The pods are tough and need long cooking. Long cooking is not a luxury everyone has fuel for.
Dense, starchy legumes packed with vegetable protein. Essential for hearty survival potages and brines.
A sealed clay pot of raw golden comb honey from the greenhouse apiary. High calorie density and natural morale booster.
A dense yellow block of rendered beeswax. Used for waterproofing textiles, candle casting, and sealing preservation jars.
Sticky antimicrobial resin harvested from beehive frames. Formulated into salves to treat burns and infected wounds.
Strained washings of honey combs and clean water prepared for crock fermentation into celebratory mead.
Crushed and graded rock salt from subterranean veins. Essential for curing meats, brining vegetables, and curing hides.
A heavy 25kg burlap sack of weighed halite crystals stamped by the weigh-hut. Universal inland barter currency.
Recrystallized medical-grade sodium chloride used in sterile IV solutions, wound washes, and burn irrigation.
Crisp sliced tubers cured in saline brine and wild mustard seed. Stable for months in pantry storage.

Bracket mushrooms from the tunnel beds, sliced thin and dried over the boiler exhaust. They taste of umami and a faint earthiness that is either the substrate or the air in the lower corridors — nobody is entirely sure. Rehydrated in boiling water they plump to something almost satisfying. The Rot Farmers sell dried mushrooms as their primary export. The Botanist grows them as a supplement. The distinction matters to both of them.

Strips of surface-trapped animal protein, smoked over chips of compressed peat and birch bark in the smokehouse behind the generator room. The smoking is long and low, enough to dry the meat to a dark leather that keeps for two weeks without refrigeration. What kind of animal it was is not always specified. The flavor varies by season and by what the surface patrols were able to bring back. Nobody asks too many questions about the meat.
Boiled ash-grain and tuber stew sealed in sanitized tin containers. Maximum shelf life during deep winter.
Dense strips of meat packed in coarse halite salt. Tough to chew unless soaked, but virtually impervious to decay.

Animal fat, rendered clean and used to slow-cook and preserve protein strips submerged in the fat itself. The result stores at cellar temperature for three weeks and provides both the protein and the fat in one dense serving. The Steward rations it carefully because the fat is used for cooking, for lamps, and for waterproofing the outer gear. Three purposes for one resource is the rule, not the exception.

Shredded greenhouse cabbage fermented in salt brine in a sealed ceramic crock. The fermentation produces lactic acid that preserves the cabbage and creates a dense vitamin C source at almost no fuel cost. The smell permeates the food storage room for two days after a batch is opened. The smell is exactly what you expect. The taste is sharper and better than you expect the first time.
Boiled fruit mash preserved in raw honey syrup. A rare sweet treat that lifts morale across the shelter.
Sanitized packets of dried yarrow and fever-bark. Infused in hot water for fever relief and soothing warmth.
Salt-brined pea paste in sealed stoneware crocks. High vegetable protein source when meat is scarce.
Multi-stage sintered ceramic filter cartridge with silver impregnation. Strips 99.9% of suspended radioactive particulate from tainted water.
Composite panel of borated polymer and lead foil laminate for lining bunker bulkheads and medical ward walls against gamma wash.

A military respirator with an upgraded seal gasket and an additional over-pressure valve that prevents fogging. The original mask was designed for chemical protection and was not rated for the combination of particulate and radiological exposure that the current environment requires. Someone has fitted a secondary charcoal sleeve over the main filter housing and replaced the head straps with nylon webbing. It works better than the original. The modifications are documented on a card taped inside the carry case.
Heavy-duty 24V inverter module converting erratic DC photovoltaic output into clean AC power for sensitive bunker electronics.
Precision brass rotor from a pre-war encryption transceiver. Allows automated frequency-hopping and cryptographically secure communications.

A pleated glass-fiber HEPA filter cartridge for bunker intake fans. It traps particles down to 0.3 microns — fine enough to catch ash and fallout dust, not fine enough to catch vapors. The gray pleating turns black in a month under heavy load. When the pressure differential rises past the red mark, it is clogged and the shelter is breathing through it like a man with wet cloth over his mouth. You do not want to be in the bunker when someone forgets to change it.
Autoclaved surgical toolkit containing precision scalpels, titanium hemostats, vascular clamps, and sterile needle drivers.
Distilled lab-grade organic solvent and chemical precursor for synthesizing medical antibiotics and chelation compounds.
Heavy pressure-sealed rubberized diving suit with brass helmet collar for deep submerged maritime salvage runs.
Pressurized pyrotechnic canister containing silver iodide flare compound to induce atmospheric precipitation over fallout plumes.
High-sensitivity ground vibration probe for detecting subterranean structural shifts, mining cave-ins, and surface raider convoys.
Thick waterproof field notebook documenting mutation phenotypes, edible flora, and hazard evasion protocols.
High-temperature cutting lance rig utilizing pressurized oxygen and burning magnesium rods to melt through blast doors.

A replacement logic board for the automated sentry turret's targeting system. The original chip failed to distinguish between threat and non-threat at ranges under fifteen meters, which became a problem. The replacement chip has a broader threat classification protocol and a two-second confirmation delay before firing. The Electrician installed it herself. She does not describe the testing process in her maintenance log.
Miniaturized semiconductor gamma detector with real-time digital dose rate readouts and cumulative ledger logging.
Militarized glass triode tube engineered for ultra-low noise amplification in harsh electromagnetic environments.

A lead-acid battery that has been drained, flushed, and recharged with fresh electrolyte to restore partial capacity. The original cells had sulfated plates that were ground back with abrasive compound. The reconditioned battery holds about sixty percent of its rated charge and is not suitable for starting motors. It is perfectly suitable for radios, lights, and everything else that cannot afford to wait for a new battery that does not exist.
Chelated mineral salts and micro-nutrients formulated to accelerate root growth in closed-loop bunker trays.

A sealed transceiver module from a military communication system, still in its rubberized shock housing. The module covers the tactical frequency bands and includes a built-in encryption chip that no longer has anyone to encrypt to. The Wire Heads use the module for its transmitter stage — more wattage per battery than anything civilian, and EMP hardened by design. The encryption key is still set to a code from before the Exchange. Nobody has changed it.
Phosphor CRT display tube from an airport Doppler radar console, capable of plotting distant atmospheric storm tracks.
High-pressure fluid actuator rated for 5-ton force output in heavy machinery, deep-well pumps, and exo-frames.
Encrypted friend-or-foe transponder emitting authenticated beacon responses to neutralize automated sentry guns.
Military respirator cartridge offering Level-A protection against persistent biological aerosols and nerve agents.

A motorized joint actuator salvaged from a robotic surgical assistant. The servo provides precise, tremor-free movement and is rated for continuous operation over a six-hour procedure. The surgical assistant it came from was destroyed in the first winter. The servo survived because it was stored in its shipping case in the supply room. The doctor uses it as a retractor during complex procedures. She calls it the most useful thing in the medical bay that she did not train on.
Manual double-seam can sealer and pressure vessel for hermetically sealing food tins without electricity.

A twist of copper wire shaped into a loose loop and pegged to the ground. The poorest survivor's option, better than doing nothing. It breaks often, catches little, and costs almost nothing to replace.
A wooden box with a gravity door, triggered by a treadle inside. Bulky, dependable, and shelter-craftable. The workhorse once the bunker can afford one.
A woven funnel of wood and cord set in moving water. Fish enter but cannot find the exit. Strong where geography supports it, worthless where it does not.
A heavy spring-loaded mechanism that closes steel jaws on anything that passes through the frame. Efficient, durable, and severe. Manufactured before the exchange, or found in trapper caches.
A loop of cord or wire set across a game trail, tightened by a springy branch. Cheap enough to deploy more than one, unreliable enough that materials still matter.
A flat stone or salvaged plate balanced on a trigger stick. Low-tech, material-light, and as old as hunger. The trigger is the hard part.
A concealed pit dug into a game trail, lined with sharpened stakes. Labor-heavy, location-dependent, and capable of stopping something large.
A mesh of cord or salvaged netting strung between posts or branches. Broader coverage than a snare, higher upfront cost, and more things can go wrong.
A sprung cage of salvaged metal and wire, triggered by weight on a plate. Expensive to build, durable once built. The animal lives inside it.
A fine noose of thread or thin wire set on a perch stick. Lightweight, fast to deploy, and fragile. Frequent small calories with a health-risk shadow.
A carefully sleeved classical record with a split paper jacket. A hand-written listening date is inked on the inner sleeve in small, deliberate handwriting.
A government instructional recording pressed on heavy vinyl. The label bears a municipal crest and a serial number stamped in red ink.
A worn compilation from a small regional label. The sleeve art shows a river bend and a painted sunset. Someone traced the track listing in pencil.
A faded photograph of three people in ordinary clothing. One face is circled in blue ink on the reverse. The edge is creased from a wallet fold.
A group portrait in front of a concrete wall. Unit insignia is visible on shoulder patches. Someone wrote names on the back in three different hands.
A printed poster showing shelter procedures with numbered diagrams. The corners are torn where it was ripped from a wall. The ink is still bright.
A large-format poster with bold typography and a factory silhouette. The slogan is half-obscured by a water stain that runs diagonally across the lower third.
A hand-lettered poster for a community hall concert. The date and venue are legible. Someone added a phone number in marker at the bottom.
A soft-cover manual with dog-eared pages and a coffee ring on the back cover. The spine is reinforced with medical tape. Diagrams show wound closure and splinting.
A paperback with a cracked spine and a bookmark left at page 84. The cover shows a painted landscape that no longer exists. The pages smell of dust and old paper.
A damaged issue with a marked technical article on water purification. Someone underlined a paragraph about filtration rates in red pencil.
An outdoors magazine with advertisements for gear that no longer exists. The cover shows a mountain lake. The pages are foxed at the edges.
A grease-stained manual with torque specifications and wiring diagrams. The cover is reinforced with duct tape. A mechanic's notes are penciled in the margins.
A spiral-bound guide with component diagrams and frequency charts. The binding is cracked and three pages are loose. Someone marked the emergency frequencies in ink.
A technical handbook with chemical dosing tables and filter maintenance procedures. The cover is water-damaged but the text is legible. Tabs mark the purification chapter.
A manufacturer's manual for HEPA filtration units. Diagrams show seal replacement and pressure-drop testing. The warranty card is still tucked inside the back cover.
A pocket-sized guide for calibrating pen dosimeters and Geiger counters. The calibration tables are printed on waterproof stock. A sticker shows a lab serial number.
A torn page from a military unit log. Dates, route codes, and supply counts are typed in columns. Three names are crossed out in blue pencil.
A carbon copy of a deployment order with unit designations and movement times. The paper is creased where it was folded into quarters. A rubber stamp mark is partially visible.
A typed list of names, service numbers, and evacuation codes. The paper is brittle and the ink has faded to brown. Someone annotated the margins in pencil.
A handwritten letter on lined paper, the script careful and slightly uneven. It asks about food, sleep, and whether the heating is working. The envelope is addressed but unsealed.
A letter folded into a small square, never posted, the handwriting hurried. It describes a cold night and a missing friend. The paper is creased from being carried in a pocket.
A form letter denying a housing application. The signature is a rubber stamp. Someone wrote 'appeal' in the margin and underlined it twice.
A metal badge with a stamped serial number and a pin-back clasp. The enamel is chipped at one edge. It identifies a civil-defense volunteer role.
A brass badge with a transit authority crest. The pin is bent but the engraving is clear. It marks a municipal worker or inspector.
An embroidered shoulder patch with a unit insignia. The thread is frayed at the edges where it was pulled from a uniform. The colors are still distinct.
A woven patch showing a gear and hammer crossed. The backing is stiff with old adhesive. It marks a maintenance or trade guild member.
A cloth doll with button eyes and yarn hair. One arm is reattached with rough stitching. The dress is made from a scrap of patterned fabric.
A small tin music box with a painted lid. The mechanism still turns when wound, though the melody is simple and slightly out of tune. The key is bent but functional.
A small devotional book with a worn leather cover. The pages are thin and the text is printed in two columns. A ribbon marker is sewn into the spine.
A string of wooden beads with a metal cross or medallion. The wood is smooth from handling. The cord is knotted at intervals and shows wear at the clasp.
A triangular pennant in washed-out team colors. The felt is soft and the stitching is loose at one corner. A date and score are printed below the team name.
A folded program for a local sports match. Player names and positions are listed inside. The cover shows a team logo and a sponsor's advertisement.
A brass token stamped with a civic crest and a festival date. The edge is milled and the surface shows light corrosion. It was a souvenir or admission token.
A small ceramic tile with a painted landscape. The glaze is crackled and one corner is chipped. The painting shows a village scene with a church spire.
A newspaper from the day of the exchange. The headline is partially visible through a water stain. The paper is brittle and the edges crumble when handled.
An ordinary local paper from before the crisis. The front page shows sports scores, a weather forecast, and a classified ad for a used car. Nothing apocalyptic.
A folded road map with routes highlighted in yellow marker. The folds are worn through at the creases. Someone circled a junction and wrote 'check this' in pencil.
A military topographic map with contour lines and grid references. The paper is waterproof stock. Annotations show patrol routes and observation posts in red ink.
A hand-drawn map on the back of a utility bill. Landmarks are sketched in pencil with notes about danger zones and water sources. The handwriting is cramped and urgent.
A carbon-copy roster with names crossed out in different inks. Some names were added after the original typing. The last page is blank except for a date stamp.
A ruled ledger with increasingly uneven handwriting. Serving weights are recorded in columns that grow narrower toward the back cover.
A folded clinical note found along a corridor. The paper is creased from being carried in a pocket. One corner is stained dark.
A rough sketch of numbered barricade locations drawn on the back of a municipal form. One route is circled twice in red.
A printed warning notice taped over a door frame. Someone has written additional instructions in marker beneath the official text.
A photograph with writing on the reverse. The image shows three people standing in front of a building that no longer exists. The paper is soft from handling.
A folded topographic map with grease-pencil deployment marks. The annotations contradict the printed legend in several places.
A typed broadcast script with corrections in two different hands. Several lines are struck through before the final version.
A faction poster written over by multiple hands in different inks. The original message is barely visible beneath the responses.
A piece of cardboard with a warning written in charcoal. The letters are large and deliberate. Wire is threaded through a hole punched in one corner.
A clipboard with a maintenance checklist. The same temporary repair is signed off six times in different handwriting. The seventh slot is empty.
A typed admission list with reason codes beside each name. The codes are administrative: CAPACITY, MEDICAL, SECURITY, DEFERRED. Several names have no code at all.
A small notebook comparing expected and actual stock levels. The discrepancies are recorded without comment. The last entry is dated three days before the final supply drop.
An official notice posted beside a water source. A handwritten correction has been added below the printed text, contradicting the all-clear date.
A repair checklist that ends mid-procedure. The last completed step is circled twice. The pen mark trails off the edge of the paper.
A typed list of names with status columns. The categories shift partway through — from MEDICAL to MISSING to simply a dash. The typing becomes uneven.
A treatment priority sheet with numbered strips of cardboard attached. The numbers correspond to patients who are no longer present. The saline bags above are empty.
A letter folded into an envelope that was never sealed. The handwriting is careful at the beginning and rushed at the end. No address is written on the front.
A requisition form with SUBSTITUTED stamped across the original request. The approved items are less than half of what was requested. The signature is illegible.
A public evacuation map with handwritten blocked-route markings. Three of the four printed routes are crossed out. A fourth route has been added in pencil.
A printed quarantine notice with a date and time. A second notice has been stapled over it with tighter restrictions. The staples are rusted.
A pre-crisis civil defense poster listing emergency procedures. The advice is practical and calm. Someone has written 'GOOD LUCK' in the margin.
A concise operational report typed on a manual typewriter. The margins contain handwritten annotations in a different hand. One paragraph is underlined twice.
A few torn pages from a personal journal. The entries describe small routines — meals, weather, a broken window. The last entry stops mid-sentence.
An official death certificate with several blank fields. The cause-of-death line contains a question mark. The signature block is empty.
An inventory sheet showing expected and actual stock. One crate is listed as MISSING with a note: 'See Requisition 4471.' The requisition number does not appear elsewhere.
A handwritten log of radio frequencies and times. The entries stop on a specific date. The last entry reads: '142.5 — no response. 88.4 — static. 104.7 — silence.'
A child's drawing on lined paper. The figures are tall and the house is small. A sun occupies the entire upper corner. Labels are written in an adult's hand beneath the child's marks.
A confession written on the back of a utility form. The handwriting is steady. The author names a specific action, a specific place, and a specific consequence. Nothing else.
A will written on lined paper and witnessed by two signatures. The author assigns specific items to specific people. One name has been crossed out and replaced.
A printed notice from a creditor faction declaring the shelter in default. The notice lists the debt amount, the missed deadline, and the consequences. A stamp reads FINAL NOTICE in red ink.
A weather-beaten notice posted at a route entrance. The lamination is cracked and water has seeped in. The warning advises against travel.
A typed patrol order from a faction commander. The order specifies the patrol route, rules of engagement, and what to look for. Margins contain handwritten annotations.
A thick, dense wool overcoat tailored to withstand biting subzero blizzards.
Pre-war arctic exploration parka filled with thermal synthetic down.
Heavy fur gauntlets that protect fingers from cold-numbness and frostbite.
Double-felt insulated snow boots with deep rubber treads.
A perforated 55-gallon steel drum rigged for emergency scrap wood burning.
A portable convection kerosene space heater capable of warming bunker rooms.
A weathered acoustic guitar strung with scavenged wire strings.
A pocket brass diatonic harmonica in the key of C.
A complete deck of 52 cards used for poker, blackjack, and solitary patience.
A small animal or figure hand-carved from scrap wood during downtime hours.
A sketch of the surface or shelter life drawn on reclaimed cardstock.
Notched military identification tags worn by high-value targets or officers.
A notched branding iron or insignia carried by wasteland gang leaders as proof of authority.
A magnetic keycard containing pre-war military decryption tokens and algorithmic hashes.
Tempered surgical steel saw with fine serrations used for rapid traumatic amputations.
Concentrated analgesic tablets that mitigate traumatic surgical shock and severe nerve pain.
A carved pine prosthetic arm with articulated copper joints and leather straps.
A reinforced oak peg leg with rubber foot tread, restoring mobility after lower limb loss.
Advanced pre-war prosthetic arm with direct nerve-interface sensors and titanium servo motors.
Pre-war military bionic limb featuring pneumatic suspension and hydraulic load balancers.
High-density anthracite coal mined from subterranean seams, essential for locomotive steam boilers.
Heavy rolled steel standard gauge track section used for permanent way repairs.
Pressure-treated timber sleepers for anchoring heavy iron tracks across gravel roadbeds.
Spore inoculum for growing high-yield edible grey mycelium beds in darkness.
Rare bioluminescent fungal spores providing ambient cold illumination without electricity.
Rare mycelial strain containing antimicrobial peptides for medical drug synthesis.
Nutrient-dense cultivated caps harvested from dark underground beds. Safe to cook and consume.
Hoarded shelter emergency foodstuffs recovered as physical evidence in theft investigations.
Physical forensic evidence linking a suspect to a violent assault or sabotage site.
Reusable classroom slate used by children and apprentices for spelling and numeracy drills.
Hand-copied instructional book covering basic first aid, botany, and foraging for young dwellers.
Heavy riveted iron cuffs used to secure dangerous captives and unruly raiders in detention.
Distilled poppy and valerian extract used to pacify frantic prisoners or calm traumatized children.
Pre-war cryo-preserved viral vector used in clinical gene therapy to excise unstable DNA mutations.
Loose hooded cowl treated with fine volcanic ash to blend seamlessly into scorched wastelands.
Heavy burlap netting woven with dried reeds and marsh moss for deep concealment in wet biomes.
Matte-black rubberized jumpsuit that muffles footsteps and eliminates glare during night sorties.
Machined aluminum canister packed with steel wool baffles to suppress rifle muzzle reports.
Light-amplifying electro-optical goggles providing acute situational awareness in subterranean darkness.
Refined pressurized fuel canister suitable for ultralight combustion engines and blowtorches.
Duralumin ribs, tension cables, and treated fabric for maintaining improvised airframes.
Heavy wrought iron leg fetters and link chain used to secure captives on arduous labor details.
Heavy riveted steel collar with padlock lug, scavenged from wasteland slavers to coerce compliance.
Distilled pharmaceutical reagent base used in laboratory synthesis of advanced medicines.
Pure anhydrous solvent solution used for chemical compounding and crystalline precipitation.
Concentrated neural stimulant ampoule that accelerates reflex response at severe cardiac risk.
Potent botanical analgesic tincture that suppresses acute physical pain but induces sedation.
Refined crystalline stimulant salts that temporarily eliminate mental exhaustion.
Pungent sedative resin block vaporized to calm psychological panic and acute trauma.
Heavy welded steel ballot repository with tamper-evident seal for settlement democratic votes.
Dense unleavened bread baked from greenhouse ash-grain. Keeps for days wrapped in cloth and tastes faintly of the filter-bed soil it grew in.
Surface-foraged roots boiled clean in shelter water. Soft, bland, and safe — most days that is enough.
A hot pot of greenhouse greens and tubers simmered in clean water. Steam on the window, a bowl in every hand. The shelter feels almost whole when it is on the stove.
Smoked meat and rendered grain pressed into wax-paper blocks. A day's ration that fits in a coat pocket and outlasts the expedition that carries it.
Smoked meat, pickled tubers, and flatbread wrapped together in waxed cloth. Everything a walker needs for a long day outside the wire, packed to carry light.
A weighted coil in a spiked can. Driven into soil or bedrock, it turns the ground's shudder into a whisper of current.
A shielded preamp box wound for quiet. The hard part was never hearing; it was hearing only the ground.
Sand-filled pads and rubber gaskets that convince machinery noise to stay home instead of walking into the sensor lines.
A cased borehole string with grouting kit. Lowered, sealed, and forgotten — until the deep rock has news.
Fool's gold, so called. The acid line knows better: roasted and worked, it gives up its sulfur honestly.
A waxed-glass carboy of bench acid, packed in straw. Everyone in the shelter knows exactly which shelf it lives on.
A general-purpose oxidizing reagent for the bench train. It makes slow chemistry out of stubborn slag and old metal.
A sealed bench flask of the third fraction. Small, expensive, and never stored where a lamp could fall on it.
Fractionated acid cut to cell strength in waxed flasks. The difference between a battery and a planter box.
A dilute bath that eats scale and slag film off fresh castings. Rinsed in time, it stops where told.
Burnt lime slaked and bagged. The quiet answer to everything the acid line spills, stored within reach of the retort room.
Topped-up electrolyte blended for aging cells. The generator crew takes it without being asked twice.
Reams of buffered paper pulled from a printer's warehouse before the roof fell in. Cultural work runs on this: transcription, chronicles, testimony kept past the life of the people in it.
Sealed high-contrast film for the archive camera. Each sheet holds a shelf of books at stamp size. Keep it cold, keep it dark, keep it away from the flood line.
Aluminum blanks coated in black lacquer. The cutting stylus carves sound straight into the surface — one pass, no second takes. The archive calls them fragile; the musicians call them proof.
Battery round with a clockwork fuse set by hand. Fills the sky with fragments on a schedule. Heavy, loud, and the closest thing to an umbrella the shelter owns.
The fuse listens for the target and decides on its own. Rarer than the flak rounds and worth the trouble: it does not need the gunner's guess to be perfect.
A dense dart behind a powder charge, for things that fall too fast and too straight. Three to a crate, each one accounted for in the ledger.
A cloud of foil strips fired ahead of the track to confuse the incoming seeker. Stops nothing by itself; buys the gun crews the seconds that do.
Burns bright and orange where it bursts, marking the track for guns that lost it. Nobody's favorite round. Everybody's when the fog closes in.
Copper liner, cavity forward, all the promise of a cutting torch at terminal velocity. For the heavy tracks that shrug at fragments.
Dark flour milled from ash-barley grain. It is coarse, shelf-stable, and suitable for the shelter kitchen's bread and porridge recipes.
A sealed maintenance packet used by the grain authority to lower normalized silo pest pressure.
A sealed medical oxygen supply unit produced by the shelter's abstract air-separation plant.
A sealed nitrogen supply unit used as a general foundry and workshop process input.
Crude mined rock salt crystals used as electrochemical feedstock for chlor-alkali sanitation chemistry.
Concentrated sodium hypochlorite solution produced by the chlor-alkali plant for water disinfection and medical hygiene.
Solid sodium hydroxide byproduct used in industrial soap synthesis, scrubbing, and chemical neutralization.
Dimensionally stable dimensioned anode plate used in high-purity chlor-alkali synthesis cells.
Precision-stamped polished aluminum curved segment for assembling high-temperature solar concentrators.
Motorized or counterweighted mechanical mount that keeps optical concentrators aligned with the sun.
Closed-cycle heat engine mounted at a solar dish focal point to generate electricity from concentrated sunlight.
Annealed thick glass disc with low thermal expansion, ready for rough grinding, polishing, and parabolization.
Ultra-fine optical polishing compound used to achieve scratch-free optical surfaces and figure correction.
Channelled optical pitch tool cast on a backing plate, used for precision parabolization and figuring.
Optical bench knife-edge testing apparatus for quantitative shadowgram surface figure measurement.
Heavy reinforced tactical breaching shield offering high frontal kinetic protection and anchorable phalanx defense.
Multi-layer polycarbonate-glass composite viewport insert providing optical clarity under tactical fire.
Tungsten-tipped deployable anchor spikes allowing tactical shields to lock into concrete or frozen earth.
